question.text: Cutaneous melanoma in a multiethnic population: is this a different disease?
question.context: Cutaneous melanoma in nonwhite persons has a manifestation and a prognosis that are different than those of cutaneous melanoma in white persons. Case series. Tertiary care university-affiliated community medical center located in a multiethnic state in which white persons are a minority of the population. Consecutive series of 357 patients with melanoma seen between January 1994 and August 2003. Ethnicity, age, sex, primary site, tumor thickness, nodal status, stage at diagnosis, and survival. There were 208 men and 149 women who ranged in age from 15 to 93 years (mean, 58 years). Twenty-two patients initially had unknown primary sites. Of these 357 patients, 67 (18.7%) were nonwhite. There was no statistically significant difference in the age (P =.10) or sex (P =.57) distribution of these 2 populations. Nonwhite patients at initial diagnosis had thicker tumors (P =.002), more frequently had ulcerated primary tumors (P<.001), more frequently had positive nodes (P =.004), and were at a more advanced stage (P =.002) than their white counterparts. The anatomic distribution between the 2 populations was significantly different (P<.001), with a high incidence of melanoma on the sole and subungual locations and a substantially less frequent occurrence on the head and neck, trunk, and extremities in the nonwhite population when compared with the white population. The overall survival rate of the nonwhite patients was significantly worse than that of the white patients, but when stratified by stage at initial diagnosis, there was no difference in outcome.

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The clinical case demonstrates that cutaneous melanoma in nonwhite individuals presents with distinct characteristics compared to white individuals, including thicker tumors, more frequent ulceration, positive nodes, and advanced stage at diagnosis. These differences in presentation and prognosis suggest that it is a different disease, even if the survival rate is not significantly different when stratified by stage.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: Nonwhite patients at initial diagnosis had thicker tumors (P =.002), more frequently had ulcerated primary tumors (P<.001), more frequently had positive nodes (P =.004), and were at a more advanced stage (P =.002) than their white counterparts.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: While the overall survival rate is similar when stratified by stage, the differences in presentation and prognosis suggest that the underlying disease process is distinct. Other conditions that might mimic melanoma, such as basal cell carcinoma or squamous cell carcinoma, were not considered as the case specifically focuses on melanoma.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The data shows nonwhite patients had thicker tumors, more ulceration, more positive nodes, and advanced stage at diagnosis compared to white patients. These are all prognostically significant factors associated with worse outcomes. The overall survival was significantly worse despite similar stage distribution, indicating the disease manifests differently in nonwhite populations.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: The significantly worse overall survival rate despite similar stage distribution at diagnosis demonstrates that melanoma in nonwhite populations has a different prognosis.
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: No differential diagnoses needed - this is a descriptive epidemiological study showing ethnic differences in melanoma presentation and outcome, not a case requiring differential diagnosis.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study demonstrates significant differences in tumor thickness, ulceration, nodal status, stage at diagnosis, and anatomic distribution between nonwhite and white patients with cutaneous melanoma. These differences are clinically meaningful and associated with worse overall survival in nonwhite patients, suggesting distinct disease behavior. The lack of difference in survival when stratified by stage implies biological or environmental factors beyond staging contribute to disparities.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: Nonwhite patients had thicker tumors, more ulceration, more positive nodes, and were at more advanced stage at diagnosis, with significantly worse overall survival — indicating a different disease presentation and outcome.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Considered whether these differences were due to referral bias or socioeconomic factors, but the study controlled for stage and found no difference in survival by stage, supporting biological or etiological differences rather than purely systemic bias.

olmo3_7b.critical_evidence: Nonwhite patients at initial diagnosis had thicker tumors (P = .002), more frequently had positive nodes (P = .004), were at a more advanced stage (P = .002), and had a significantly worse overall survival.
olmo3_7b.differential_considered: Possible differentials include genetic variations or environmental exposures unique to nonwhite populations, but the clinical evidence of thicker tumors, advanced stage, and worse survival in nonwhite patients directly points to a different clinical presentation and prognosis, not a different disease entity per se, but likely differences in risk factors or biology affecting melanoma behavior.
